# Writing the copy

How this project writes the text of its interface. Read it before adding or changing an entry in the catalog: `prosebook lint` checks what can be checked, after the fact, and this says it before.

## Where it goes

Every string a person reads is an entry in the catalog, `copy/catalog/<area>.yaml`, written in English. A key's first segment names its file: `cart.items` lives in `cart.yaml`. Code reads the entry by its key; text a person reads is never a literal in the code.

An entry says about itself:

- `en` (required): the message, in ICU MessageFormat.
- `context` (required): one sentence telling a translator where the string appears and what it answers to.
- `args` (required): what each placeholder holds, one line each, for every placeholder.
- `kind`: what sort of string it is, below.
- `surface`: where it sits, below.
- `fragment`: `true` where it completes something beside it, so the sentence rules leave it alone.

## Kinds

- `name`: Identifies a thing so it can be found again. One to four words, a noun phrase, no period. Held to: at most 4 words; no period at the end; no explanation after a dash or a colon; sentence case.
- `action`: Says what pressing it does. One to three words, verb first, no period. Held to: at most 3 words; no period at the end; sentence case.
- `description`: Adds only what the name cannot carry. One sentence, two at most, with a period. Held to: at most 2 sentences; ends with a period.
- `state`: Reports what is true right now. One sentence, present tense; on an error or empty state, one more saying what to do. Held to: at most 1 sentence (2 sentences on error, empty, hint and status); ends with a period on hint, status, error, empty and confirm.

Articles, short prepositions and asides in parentheses don't count as words.
In sentence case, these keep their capitals: `Corner` and `Shop`.

## Surfaces

- `action`: The text of a button or a menu entry.
- `aria`: Reached only by a screen reader, so nothing on screen carries it.
- `choice`: One option among a set offered together.
- `confirm`: The question of a confirmation, or the verb that answers it.
- `empty`: Fills a list or a panel that has nothing in it.
- `error`: Says what failed.
- `heading`: Heads a section, group, dialog or list.
- `hint`: A subordinate line under the thing it qualifies.
- `label`: Names a control, a field, a section or a destination.
- `placeholder`: Sits inside an empty field, and goes when typing starts.
- `status`: Reports what is true right now, on a badge or beside a row.
- `title`: The title of a page, window or document.
- `toast`: A notification that comes and goes.
- `tooltip`: Appears on hover.

## Words

- No leading, trailing or doubled spaces.
- Never write these, for the reason beside each:
  - `seamless`, `seamlessly`, `effortless`, `effortlessly`, `hassle-free`, `frictionless`: promises a feeling rather than saying what happens.
  - `leverage`, `leverages`, `leveraging`, `utilize`, `utilizes`, `utilizing`, `harness`, `take advantage of`: is a long way to say use.
  - `delve`, `dive into`, `deep dive`, `embark`, `journey`, `tapestry`, `realm`, `landscape`, `testament`, `synergy`, `paradigm`, `holistic`: is filler, not a thing on the screen.
  - `robust`, `powerful`, `cutting-edge`, `state-of-the-art`, `best-in-class`, `world-class`, `next-generation`, `revolutionary`, `game-changing`: is marketing: say what it does.
  - `streamline`, `streamlined`, `empower`, `unlock`, `unleash`, `elevate`, `supercharge`, `boost`, `enhance`, `enhanced`: claims an improvement without naming it.
  - `meticulous`, `crucial`, `pivotal`, `vital`, `paramount`: tells the reader how to feel instead of what it is.
  - `comprehensive`, `myriad`, `plethora`, `a variety of`, `a wide range of`: is padding: name the things, or say how many.
  - `furthermore`, `moreover`, `additionally`, `in order to`, `please note`, `note that`, `keep in mind`, `rest assured`: is a connective a short string has no room for.
  - `intuitive`, `sleek`, `stunning`, `beautiful`, `delightful`, `magical`: grades the product instead of describing it.
  - `simply`, `just`, `easily`, `easy`, `quickly`: says it is easy, which helps nobody it is not easy for.
  - `so you can`, `allows you to`, `lets you`, `enables you to`, `don't worry`: justifies or reassures: state the fact.
  - `please`, `oops`, `whoops`, `sorry`: pleads or apologizes: say what failed and what to do.
  - `etc`, `and more`, `and so on`: trails off: name the things or stop.
- Spell color (not colour), colors (not colours), behavior (not behaviour), favorite (not favourite), canceled (not cancelled), canceling (not cancelling), labeled (not labelled), center (not centre), license (not licence), gray (not grey), organize (not organise), recognize (not recognise), customize (not customise), optimize (not optimise), minimize (not minimise), maximize (not maximise), synchronize (not synchronise), authorize (not authorise), initialize (not initialise), analyze (not analyse), catalog (not catalogue), dialog (not dialogue), artifact (not artefact), judgment (not judgement), while (not whilst) and among (not amongst).
- Write `could not`, `is not` and `cannot` as contractions: couldn't, isn't, can't.
- No em-dashes, and no spaced hyphen standing in for one: a comma, a period or a colon does the job.
- An ellipsis is one character, …, not three periods.
- A path through menus or settings is written with a spaced ›: Settings › General.

## Messages

- A count beside a noun is a plural, never `{count} files`, which reads "1 files":

  ```
  {count, plural, one {# file} other {# files}}
  ```

- A plural's `one` arm writes `#`, not 1, since one is not only 1 in every language, and says something other than `other` does.
- The arms of a plural or select end alike: all with a stop, or all without one.
- Never type a currency symbol or `%` beside a placeholder, or group digits by hand (`10,000`): format the placeholder, which writes them as the locale does. A percent takes the fraction, 0.5 for 50%.

  ```
  {price, number, ::currency/EUR}
  {rate, number, percent}
  {n, number}
  ```

- A translation ends with a stop where its source does, and without one where it doesn't.

## Before you finish

- Run `prosebook lint` and fix what it finds; `prosebook lint --fix` writes the fixes it offers. Where a rule is wrong about an entry, exempt the entry under `allow` with the reason, a sentence a reviewer can check.
- `comment` and `remove` on an entry are requests from whoever looked at it last: make the change, then delete the field.
- A new or changed source leaves its translations missing or stale: `prosebook todo <locale>` lists them.
- `prosebook check` runs it all, as CI does.
